summary:
Yalova is a province of Turkey and stands under Turkey's national framework on gender identity and sexual orientation. No trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern, police practice or incident documentation exists for Yalova in the available sources. That gap is recorded as absence of documented divergence rather than evidence of local permissiveness: the national rules and the national enforcement climate apply in Yalova as they apply across Turkey.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality", carrying up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies, carrying up to four years.

The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, behind a mandatory permanent infertility assessment and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible.

Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft. Human Rights Watch warned that the measure would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest.

Kaos GL's 2025 review, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people in Turkey became explicit state policy during the year. Instructions framed around protecting "the family" were issued to public institutions, an LGBTI+ rights organisation was closed for the first time in years, expression and artistic freedom were restricted, and events were cancelled or banned.

The Kaos GL review records six right-to-life violations, including three hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected, and 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year.

It also records 313 liberty violations, about two and a half times the previous year's total, with 299 detention decisions; private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy; and 61 travel bans.
tangentialFactors:
As of the 29 October 2025 reporting, the 11th Judicial Package remained a leaked draft rather than enacted law. Its subsequent fate is not sourced here, and the pending status of the package has not been treated as a reason to discount the risk it describes.

No source in the inventory provides a provincial breakdown for Turkey. The violation counts, the draft provisions and the policy directives are national figures, so they cannot be attributed to Yalova specifically or read as a measure of conditions in Yalova alone.

The pattern of the reporting is that stated policy and enforcement practice move together rather than sequentially: Kaos GL documents restrictions on expression, event bans and detentions during the same period in which the legislative package was still under consideration.

Yalova-specific comparison is unavailable. There is no sourced record indicating whether LGBTI+ people in Yalova face more or less police attention than the national figures imply, and no reporting that would place Yalova outside the national pattern.
localsOnly:
Residents of Yalova live under the same proposed care restrictions as the rest of Turkey. If the draft provisions are enacted, the age floor for gender-affirming care including surgery rises from 18 to 25, with a mandatory permanent infertility assessment and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals, and healthcare professionals performing the procedures face fines and up to seven years in prison while patients face up to three years.

Kaos GL documents obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy as a private-life violation in 2025, one of the drivers of the rise from 16 to 67 such violations in a year. Residents seeking transition-related care are therefore dealing with documented interference in treatment, not only with a proposal.

The 299 detention decisions and 313 liberty violations recorded for 2025 are the environment residents move through, as are the 61 travel bans. An LGBTI+ rights organisation was also closed during the year, and instructions framed around protecting "the family" were issued to public institutions, which shapes how public-sector workers treat LGBT residents.

The six right-to-life violations, including three hate-motivated killings, and the rise in torture or ill-treatment violations from 51 to 89 apply to residents of Yalova as citizens of the same national jurisdiction.
